claims.text: The initial alloy is equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW.
Conventional coarse-grained NbMoTaW has limited room-temperature ductility.
NbMoTaW has excellent high-temperature mechanical strength, including at approximately 1600 °C.
The irradiation resistance of NbMoTaW has previously been assessed only computationally rather than experimentally.
The proposed intervention is room-temperature severe plastic deformation, such as high-pressure torsion, followed immediately by annealing at approximately 600 °C for about 1 hour under inert gas.
Severe plastic deformation followed by low-temperature annealing will form a high density of nanotwins and subgrain boundaries in NbMoTaW.
The nanotwins and subgrain boundaries will increase dislocation mobility and provide enhanced dislocation sources.
The nanotwins and subgrain boundaries will act as sinks for irradiation-induced defects.
The refined substructure will facilitate irradiation-defect recombination and accelerate healing of irradiation damage.
The proposed treatment will preserve the BCC phase of NbMoTaW.
Retention of a coarse overall BCC matrix will preserve high-temperature mechanical performance after processing.
Treated NbMoTaW will have significantly greater room-temperature tensile ductility than untreated NbMoTaW.
Treated NbMoTaW will have lower post-irradiation defect density than untreated NbMoTaW.
Treated NbMoTaW will suffer only minimal loss of compressive strength at 1600 °C relative to untreated NbMoTaW.
Annealing near 600 °C is sufficiently low to avoid grain growth that would eliminate the nanotwins.
Related refractory high-entropy alloys exhibit helium-energy regimes in which blistering and irradiation-induced precipitation occur.
